title: Chapter 4 — Holding On
paragraphs: Mae Mon — the ninety-three-year-old grandmother who raised Sen in Chiang Mai — dies. The family gives her a three-day funeral with Pali chanting; the town lets her go. Sen does not appear. He is in his room with a bottle of rice whiskey, and he stays there. In a book about letting go, this is the chapter about the one man who cannot.

His holding on has a history: the Chiang Mai childhood apart from his siblings, the video-rental shop that the internet quietly killed, the friends who married or emigrated, a town that keeps changing around a man who wants it "to stay the way it was." Alone among Julia's informants, Sen expects no rebirth. "It's over," he says, and gives himself fifteen years.

His attachments are drawn with great tenderness: the estrangement from Gaew as her life fills with shop, husband, future; the brother-in-law Pan who calls him lazy and threatens eviction; and Chai — clinic owner, Harley rider — with whom Sen keeps a private relationship the town's categories barely name and never announce. Old flirtations with Lek persist under deference; Aung, for her part, releases her own crush on Chai with the chapter's cleanest one-liner: wanting a person is wanting to possess one more impermanent thing.

Sen is also the town's one unordained man. Noi takes novice robes again and, asked afterward what the chant taught, remembers almost nothing and returns to his video game — ordination as social fabric rather than doctrine. Sen, who drinks and finds the wat boring, respects the Buddha but not the institution, and Mae San carries the disappointment.

Ban Ko Tao supplies the counter-model. Duansri is blunt: his parents should get angry — "Sometimes you have to get angry." Jerapong offers prayer; Surree, twenty-two and dissatisfied, walks into the hospital asking for a psychologist, a request no Buddhist in Mae Jaeng makes. Moh Bom confirms the asymmetry from the clinical side: he tells Mae Jaeng families to tham jai; his Karen patients don't recall ever hearing it. Even language cooperates — the Karen Bible glosses impermanence as Ecclesiastes' "vanity," a thing to lament rather than accept.

Meanwhile the drinking escalates. Chang, home from Sydney, sees what daily eyes have normalized: yellow skin, shaking hands, whiskey at one in the afternoon. Gaew and Chai each urge him to stop, once; Sen answers that drinking lets him chuey chuey — not feel so much, just be. His parents respond with amulets and transferred merit rather than confrontation; his mother's one direct plea is refused. At a riverside dinner, Jiew and the hospital friends press Julia to do something — there is no rehab, no psychiatrist, no AA for two hundred kilometers — and the chapter leaves the reader exactly where the town is: watching, cool-hearted, while a man holds on.
